title: Comparison of entangling strategies for unitary synthesis
abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers are promising as a platform for realizing quantum computational advantage. They promise long coherence times, near all-to-all connectivity, and potential multiqubit gates as distinguishing advantages compared to competing platforms. Regarding these advantages, it is crucial to understand the trade-offs between increasing engineering complexity and actual improvements in running quantum algorithms with a more flexible gate set. In this work, we investigate this question and develop a versatile toolset to evaluate the performance of gate sets composed of native Mølmer--Sørensen multiqubit gates. To this end, we employ unitary synthesis as an application-agnostic benchmark target and identify specific hardware requirements for multiqubit gates to be advantageous.

bite.hook: New benchmarking framework identifies exact hardware criteria for multiqubit gates to beat standard two-qubit operations.
tldr: Investigated whether multiqubit gates truly justify their hardware complexity on trapped-ion quantum computers.
Developed a toolset using unitary synthesis as an application-agnostic benchmark to assess native Mølmer-Sørensen gates.
Identified specific hardware requirements where native multiqubit gates offer a clear operational advantage.
bite.whyItMatters: Trapped-ion platforms can physically entangle many qubits at once, but doing so adds engineering headaches. Pinpointing exactly when multiqubit gates provide an edge guides hardware roadmaps toward real quantum advantage.
bite.eli5: It is like choosing between having a conversation with one friend at a time or holding a group call. Group calls are harder to set up cleanly, and this research pinpoints exactly when the group call is worth the extra trouble.
